desert_p11_001.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_001.text: The blue cloth at the shelter entrance was a drying shawl. Beneath it, an old woman sat repairing the strap of a grass bundle while a boy peeled a thin strip from a reed stalk. Tuo recognised the broad felt hat before the face turned fully toward the road. Auntie Reed looked at the three carts, then at Tuo's supported foot, and asked whether the basin had finally caught her dancing. Tuo said the dancing would have been less humiliating. Han halted at the wide shoulder and came down on foot, leaving the teams where their wheels already stood soundly.

desert_p11_002.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_002.text: The shelter belonged to a seasonal matting crew from the grass village. They used it while cutting the northern crop and checking the old stores along the foot route. Auntie Reed had come on a paid fodder wagon two days earlier, bringing their own covered water skins and meal bag. The boy was her grandson, old enough to work and young enough to resent being told when to rest. Their narrow dragging line came from the grass bundle, not an injured traveller. Yue let the stopping flag lower once the last driver saw the settled halt.

desert_p11_003.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_003.text: The question had found an ordinary answer with people inside it.

desert_p11_004.speaker: tuo_yin
desert_p11_004.text: We reached the lower exchange. Your north foot path still works where it follows the outcrop, though the eastern apron has lost more support than I remembered. I placed my foot badly beside the cairn and now receive instruction from Bao at a rate I cannot recommend. We also found the roof store. Gao screened the source with Bao, took a measured part for treatment, and left a reserve. I thought you should hear that before a carrier arrives announcing we discovered a lake where your people have been walking for years.

desert_p11_005.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_005.text: Auntie Reed's eyebrows rose at roof store. She asked which outlet they meant, making Tuo describe the north gauge and squared handle. Then she laughed, not unkindly, and said the family called it the Blue Tap although almost all its paint had gone. She cleaned its settling pocket after the winter rains when the foot approach allowed. The gauge's sheltered pencil mark recorded her last visit. Du brought the copied year and initials. She identified them as her own, then pointed out a small repair detail at the overflow lip that had never entered his transcription.

desert_p11_006.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_006.text: Gao listened without turning the recognition into proof of every maintenance year. The old woman had not known anyone planned to reopen the loading apron. Travellers asked her about the causeway, the ridge, or fodder; she answered those questions. The old store served people on foot, and she never recommended loaded carts take its approach. Its water still required checking and boiling after long storage. The district had stopped paying a keeper decades earlier, but the village families continued occasional cleaning because people still used the road. Han looked back at his dispatch book. No column named that work.

desert_p11_007.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_007.text: He had recorded the quarry, carrier firms, and receiving houses as though care travelled only through offices.

desert_p11_008.speaker: han_xun
desert_p11_008.text: I should like the report to include what your crew actually maintains. We have called the place abandoned because its office closed and the roof drifted under salt. That word has been doing more work than it deserves. Tell Gao the visits you can document, and we can place them beside the source inspection. I am not asking you to promise service every season. The next proposal should not turn your unpaid work into a guarantee other people sell.

desert_p11_009.speaker: han_xun
desert_p11_009.text: If carriers want a functioning stop, they must arrange its care with the people who know it, and pay for more than a name.

desert_p11_010.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_010.text: Auntie Reed said payment was welcome but not the only issue. A reopened freight stop could crush the grass route under more wheels, draw the store dry, and leave village children carrying water farther. A repair that helped carriers could still burden the neighbours. The boy listened while coiling the peeled reed strip into a toy ring. He asked whether their company would bring roofs too. Han said a company could pay roof makers; it did not create good roofs by arriving.

desert_p11_011.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_011.text: The woman nodded, pleased that he had not answered the child with a splendid promise nobody at the table could build. Gao showed the two-site figure. Auntie Reed named the upper house and lower tap by the forms village people used, neither matching the formal labels exactly. She knew the lower service rooms existed but had never entered the glass case passage. Her maintenance stayed at the settling pocket, outlet, and visible approach. She had no authority to certify the buried hall for freight. She said this without embarrassment. Du wrote the scope beside her account.

desert_p11_012.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_012.text: The record grew less glamorous and more useful: somebody cared for specific parts of the station, while other parts remained closed to everyone present. The grandson brought a folded cloth containing two little receipts from last winter. The matting crew bought a brush, cleaning cloth, and transport space at the quarry shed. Their private purchases had supported the public store's continued use. Han read the dates and returned the receipts rather than treating the documents as finds for his report case. Gao copied the details with Auntie Reed's permission and wrote where the originals remained.

desert_p11_013.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_013.text: Yue watched the boy fold the cloth carefully. His grandmother's work had begun appearing on a page strangers might value, but the actual papers still belonged beside her meal bag.

desert_p11_014.speaker: gao_ru
desert_p11_014.text: We shall identify your account as a present statement supported by these receipts and the site details you supplied. The old pencil mark matches your copy; its existence does not tell us every condition between visits. Our own inspection covers what we saw yesterday and today. Put those together and a later team gains a sensible history to check. Keep the originals dry. If the collective joins the new work, the station's maintenance record should have a home where your people can read it, instead of vanishing into a carrier cupboard whenever it becomes useful.

desert_p11_015.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_015.text: The old woman asked whether they had left the outlet properly capped. Han described the closing draw, and Gao showed the gauge note with its estimated reserve. Auntie Reed approved leaving accessible water rather than emptying the source for a longer inspection. She intended to check the pocket tomorrow with her grandson, taking only their ordinary needs after a fresh visual look and treatment. The main catchment would collect future rain when rain actually came. She did not predict the season's yield.

desert_p11_016.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_016.text: Yue heard someone who had lived with the store for years decline the easy comfort of saying it would always provide. The boy wanted to know how many rooms lay under the apron. Du said the standard plan showed several spaces, but later changes and drifting made the present count uncertain. The boy looked disappointed until Yue offered the exterior sketch. He followed its line with a reed ring, moving from the gauge to the three openings. He had imagined one cellar full of pots. The drawing gave him several functions without making them a secret palace.

desert_p11_017.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_017.text: Auntie Reed told him to keep his curiosity above ground until the proper inspection. He said she had been curious below ground first, which she admitted with a laugh. The grandson unfolded a scrap of wrapping paper and asked Du whether he could learn to make a map. Auntie Reed said he ought first to learn to keep his socks where his feet could find them. Du asked which place he wished to draw. The boy pointed at their shelter, the road, and the well-used cutting ground beyond it. He did not ask for a kingdom.

desert_p11_018.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_018.text: Yue showed him how to begin with three things he could presently see, leaving imagined connections for later. He scratched the shapes in dust with a reed while she held the public sheet above the wind. His first road line passed through the shelter wall. He had drawn the wall where it looked important rather than where it stood. Yue asked him to walk the short distance between the two, then return and place it again. The corrected line looked less attractive and more usable. Du knelt carefully to examine it, minding his old knees.

desert_p11_019.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_019.text: He said mapmakers often charged much more to make the same first mistake. The boy laughed and stopped treating the imperfect drawing as a failure. Auntie Reed watched from her strap repair, interest hidden badly behind a complaint about dust on trousers.

desert_p11_020.speaker: du_she
desert_p11_020.text: Take this spare public sheet. It shows the district farther south, not the whole route we just examined. Our new correction is still a working figure. Compare the old printed road with places your grandmother knows, and write questions in the blank margin. Do not cross out her answers merely because the print looks more official. If you later come to Bitter Wells, the receiving house can tell you where the public drawing lessons meet. I shall leave a note asking whether they accept another pupil. That is an enquiry, not a seat I own and can give away.

desert_p11_021.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_021.text: The boy accepted the sheet with both hands, then tried to fold it into a smaller shape than its creases allowed. Auntie Reed intervened before he invented a new coast through the middle. She had carried maps without reading every symbol, mostly to show officials what their forms forgot. Du offered to explain the district scale. She said she understood scale well enough to know when a paper journey became a long walk. He bowed to the answer and began with the symbols instead. Yue watched two kinds of expertise negotiate a table made from a flat stone.

desert_p11_022.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_022.text: The boy wanted to know whether he could join the caravan immediately and learn while travelling. Han looked at Auntie Reed before answering. She said the northern cutting work still needed his agreed help, and his mother expected them home on the booked fodder wagon. The boy's face fell. Yue told him her own present work had begun with a paid trial, not an invitation to abandon every existing arrangement when a map became interesting. He asked how long he would have to wait.

desert_p11_023.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_023.text: She said the receiving teacher could answer about study; she could only show him a useful first exercise now. Auntie Reed softened after the boy returned to his dust drawing. She said his mother wanted him to learn sums well enough that nobody could confuse him over fodder prices. He wanted roads, which sounded to the family like the same work they already did, made more dangerous and less likely to come home for supper. Gao described the distinction between learning to observe and promising a travelling career. A child could begin locally.

desert_p11_024.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_024.text: The grandmother nodded, relieved that the advice did not require choosing between ignorance and immediate departure. Han offered the receiving-house address on the map's blank corner. Yue drew the shelter again with the boy, this time from the roadside angle. Its blue shawl made an easy landmark but would vanish as soon as his grandmother folded it. He proposed drawing it anyway. She asked what would still be there next month. He chose the low black stone beside the entrance. The lesson amused him enough that he added the shawl in a separate little picture, labelled today with Du's help.

desert_p11_025.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_025.text: A changing feature did not need to be banished from a drawing. It needed a place that told the reader how long to trust it. The old woman had completed the grass-bundle strap while they worked. She tested it by lifting a small portion, then a larger one, listening for a stitch giving way. Han noticed the sequence and asked who made the tape. The village women wove it from tougher outer fibres discarded by roof makers. It held well under steady load but disliked a sharp metal edge. She showed him the protective wrap at the buckle.

desert_p11_026.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_026.text: His next outfitter order acquired another question. The family shelter had become a source of practical things the company yard had overlooked while buying expensive failed sacks.

desert_p11_027.speaker: gao_ru
desert_p11_027.text: If the next inspection comes through your village, I want its people to hear these distinctions before the office chooses equipment. We brought service casks because the keeper happened to have them. A dedicated team should plan containers, lifting gear, paper handling, and its own return load. Your route and source knowledge belongs in that planning. We can pay field consultation without pretending it buys the land or every future answer. Will you ask the collective who they want to represent the maintenance work? Han will bring the report before anyone signs a grand reopening scheme.

desert_p11_028.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_028.text: Auntie Reed said the collective would choose someone who could sit through town meetings without throwing a bowl. She disqualified herself, then reconsidered when Tuo pointed out that honesty might be worth the risk. The grandson laughed so loudly he lost the scale sheet's corner to a gust. He caught it against his knee, copied the crease pattern carefully, and put it inside the wrapping cloth. Du looked pleased by the small correction. Yue saw how teaching could become another kind of maintenance: not making a perfect person, but giving somebody a better habit before the next wind arrived.

desert_p11_029.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_029.text: Before the caravan left, the grandmother asked Bao about Tuo's ankle in terms more direct than the guide preferred. Bao described the present findings and riding restrictions, withholding no important discomfort to preserve Tuo's pride. Auntie Reed told the guide she would expect her at the village meeting seated, not demonstrating a miraculous recovery for the tile players. Tuo said the village's sympathy remained offensively practical. The woman replied that impractical sympathy had never mended a roof. Their laughter had the age of many previous conversations.

desert_p11_030.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_030.text: Yue felt briefly outside it, then welcomed by its easy refusal to perform for strangers. The boy's final dust map showed road, shelter, black stone, and cutting ground with a small uncertain gap where the path left sight. He wanted to fill it. Du told him to ask his grandmother after packing rather than inventing the turn. The boy nodded, already bored with the advice but keeping the gap. Yue left him with that unfinished honest drawing. She did not imagine he would become a great surveyor because she had stopped beside one shelter.

desert_p11_031.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_031.text: He might study, sew, guide, or choose something nobody at the stone table had named. The little sheet made one option easier to reach. The family had their own kettle, stove fuel, and covered cups beneath the shelter wall. They offered the caravan a taste of roasted reed pith, sweet and smoky. Yue took a small piece while the cook examined the preparation with professional interest. He had known dried roots from the river but never this northern grass. Auntie Reed told him how long to roast it and what part to discard.

desert_p11_032.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_032.text: He promised nothing about selling a recipe in town. He simply asked a second question and tasted the answer. The knowledge moved between them without requiring a licence, an inscription, or a claim of discovery. Tuo remained on the cart because the shelter path was uneven. The boy brought her the roasted piece and asked how she hurt the foot. She said a stone had become unreliable while she remained overconfident. He considered that answer gravely, then said stones ought to warn people. Tuo replied that they sometimes did, in a language humans learned too slowly.

desert_p11_033.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_033.text: Bao heard and told him a staff could help translate, provided its owner listened. The child looked at Yue's borrowed staff with new interest. Yue let him examine its brass cap from the cart side, keeping the tool within reach. After asking Yue about her training and hearing the stage she had earned, he asked whether fifth stage made the staff stronger. Yue said the ash and cap retained their ordinary construction; her training concerned how she could manage small tasks with her own paired routes. His interest shifted immediately toward the routes.

desert_p11_034.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_034.text: She described them simply, without making her private method a performance for the shelter. He said his grandmother's knots also had outward and returning lines. Auntie Reed laughed and told him not to apply for a cultivation licence on the strength of a reed ring. Yue liked the comparison more than the grander questions people asked about power. Han offered to pay for the food sample, but Auntie Reed waved him off. She preferred that he tell the collective about the carrier proposal before the town offices finalised it.

desert_p11_035.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_035.text: He agreed to bring the exterior report and funding questions to the village on their return route. The promise was specific: a meeting and documents, not ownership of a repaired station or an answer to every future wheel. Gao added the commitment to the working page. The old woman watched him write, then said she would send her nephew to hear whether he remembered it after he reached a comfortable chair. They spent longer at the shelter than Han first intended, though not enough to threaten the next halt.

desert_p11_036.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_036.text: The stop had changed the report's source history and next commission's participants. Du crossed out a rough line naming the cistern unmaintained, replacing it with maintenance outside the formal station accounts. He showed Auntie Reed the correction. She said she cared more about the roof pocket than his adjective, but accepted the usefulness of getting it right. Yue saw a local fact become harder to erase because someone from the village had actually stood beside the page that named it. Before leaving, Gao asked whether the family had seen fresh water along the buried channel north of the loading apron.

desert_p11_037.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_037.text: Auntie Reed had noticed damp ground below the old wall the previous afternoon, unusual this late in the dry season. She had not gone under the apron to inspect it. Her account matched the direction of their own observed seam, with its time clearly earlier. The two observations strengthened the fact of change without identifying its source. Han would ask the quarry about the temporary berm. The woman requested the answer for the collective as well as the carriers. The grandson offered Yue the reed ring.

desert_p11_038.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_038.text: It was small enough to fit around two fingers and stiff enough to keep its shape for a while. She accepted after checking he meant a gift. He said he could make another faster now. In return she showed him the fish stone, which he judged a very sleepy fish. Auntie Reed said sleepy animals were often easier to carry. Yue wrapped both objects in the pack's outside cloth, allowing them to remain gifts rather than samples. The staff and route book went back into their proper places. The caravan moved toward the quarry yard.

desert_p11_039.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_039.text: The receiving clerk came out before Han reached the shade. He had seen the preliminary warning arrive with the camel rider and wanted the exact approach figure for the manager. Han handed him a copy, keeping the originals dry. Gao added the new damp-seam observation and Auntie Reed's account. The clerk read the two times carefully. Workers had completed a temporary berm at the settling basin the previous morning, he said. It sent water into an old northern channel to reduce the spill toward the causeway village. He did not know how far the northern flow had gone.

desert_p11_040.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_040.text: Gao asked for the berm work record and the channel plan. The clerk could show the dispatch order, which named the old channel but carried no recent survey of its downstream bed. The workers had followed a route shown on a retired district sheet. Du's face tightened. The same old terrain that had become a clean map line now received actual water. It might be the Stone Channel shown at the exchange, but they would not join the names by resemblance alone. Gao compared direction, landmarks, and the office code before writing a possible connection.

desert_p11_041.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_041.text: The manager needed to inspect downstream, not merely admire the berm's local success.

desert_p11_042.speaker: han_xun
desert_p11_042.text: Your people tried to spare the village a larger spill. That purpose belongs in the account. So does the missing downstream check. We observed fresh dampness at the lower exchange after the diversion began. We cannot prove the entire path from this table. We can give the manager a reason to send the proper team. Please put that reason above the expense receipts in his packet. If the berm protects one settlement by changing water elsewhere, the elsewhere needs people in the room too. The collective should receive the same current facts.

desert_p11_043.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_043.text: The clerk sent for a work foreman who had seen the berm built. He arrived with clay on his boots and an irritation that softened when Gao asked him to point rather than defend. The temporary bank directed a limited flow north through a cut that had carried winter drainage in older years. Its volume varied with the settling basin level. He could supply the measured opening and work time, but not a promise about the buried downstream route. Gao wrote both. The man's useful knowledge survived because nobody required him to become either villain or complete authority before speaking.

desert_p11_044.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_044.text: Du compared the cut's location with the Stone Channel label and old register reference. The direction fitted, though the buried section could include branches. A new survey would need actual levels between the berm and the exchange, plus the valley beyond. He offered to prepare the historical source list while Gao designed the current observations. Han asked the foreman whether the manager would permit the public warning to include the diversion's timing. The foreman said that was an office question.

desert_p11_045.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_045.text: Han nodded and addressed the clerk, keeping the technical man's answer from being turned into a refusal he had never made. At the quarry office, the clerk showed Han the manager's first success notice about the temporary berm. It said the lower spill was controlled and routine consignments could resume on the public ridge. That part might remain true. The note did not mention the northern channel because its downstream condition had not yet been checked. Gao proposed an addition rather than demanding the entire notice be destroyed.

desert_p11_046.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_046.text: Inspection should follow the new diversion; loaded traffic should stay off the buried apron meanwhile. The clerk read the wording and looked less trapped between defending a useful repair and admitting an incomplete one. The foreman said workers were tired of being summoned only when something failed. They had laboured through heat to protect the grass village, and now the survey crew arrived with another concern. Tuo answered from her chair that the village knew the work helped its causeway. It also needed to know where the diverted water went. Gratitude and further questions could share a room.

desert_p11_047.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_047.text: The man stared at her supported foot, then laughed without much pleasure. He said people usually chose one or the other. She replied that the water would not kindly follow such an easy division. Gao asked him to describe the crew's actual sequence. They raised the temporary berm first, opened the old northern cut in stages, then inspected the downstream visible ditch as far as the quarry boundary. Beyond it the channel entered drifting ground and the retired station district. He had not been given time or equipment for that section. The omission belonged in the manager's next order.

desert_p11_048.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_048.text: It did not require the foreman to claim he had inspected what lay beyond his task. Du wrote the exact boundary so nobody later shortened the account into either complete negligence or complete success.

desert_p11_049.speaker: han_xun
desert_p11_049.text: I shall put your sequence beside the observations. Your crew's useful work should remain visible, including where its instructions stopped. If a new team is hired, it needs the downstream section named, not left behind the phrase old channel cleared. I know how such phrases shrink a job while making its invoice look complete. We have paid for road reports that did the same. Give me the boundary marker number and the work day. The cooperative can ask the manager for a plan with a genuine next step rather than a debate about who deserves to be offended.

desert_p11_050.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_050.text: The foreman supplied the marker and time from his own pocket book. Its pages were dirty, with costs of nails and a child's school fee written beside work shifts. Han asked before copying the relevant line. The personal costs stayed under the folded page. Yue noticed the same division they had kept in the rescue record: the fact needed for the report did not make the whole person's life public evidence. The foreman seemed to relax when his school fee remained his own.

desert_p11_051.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_051.text: He had expected the surveyors to take the book and turn dirt into a judgement about the man holding it. Du asked whether the retired sheet used for the cut came from his current edition. The clerk produced a stamped office copy with an older district plan beneath its added quarry boundary. Du had helped compile the public ridge sheet, but this was a separate drainage source. Similar labels did not establish the same authorship. He said that plainly while comparing the symbols. Gao kept the two sources apart in the note.

desert_p11_052.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_052.text: A complicated chain of copying was emerging, with several offices using old information for new purposes. It would be easy to choose one map man as the whole chain's face. It would be inaccurate too. The clerk worried that distributing the new damp-seam observation might start another rumour about the quarry poisoning water. Bao stated the narrower evidence: the caravan had observed dampness, the isolated roof store's checked samples had passed their limited screens, and the diverted channel water had not been analysed by this crew. They had not found proof of poisoning.

desert_p11_053.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_053.text: The public warning concerned ground support and route use. The clerk wrote those distinctions into the manager's cover note. Fear of a false accusation did not require hiding a true observation. Both could be handled by preserving what the report actually said. Yue brought the two-site figure to the kitchen wall while Du copied the correction. A worker pointed at the lower exchange and asked why it looked like a cellar when her uncle had called it a house. Yue explained the buried roof and the three openings, using the visible facts rather than the entire manual.

desert_p11_054.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_054.text: The woman nodded and said people named places by the part that sheltered them. Her uncle slept under the east arch once. The name was understandable. It still failed as a drawing instruction for loaded carts. Du added the local name beside the formal one, not in place of it. The onion seller insisted the cook take the outer skins for a broth colour she favoured. He asked whether she expected them to travel well. She said they weighed little and cost less than his suspicious face.

desert_p11_055.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_055.text: He agreed to take the onions with the skins and went to fetch the food purse, adding no expert fee for the advice. Their argument sounded like the same trade anywhere, familiar enough that Yue felt homesick for rooms she had never lived in. The quarry's official story concerned banks and consignments. Its kitchen carried another story, maintained through meals that workers expected whether the manager's repair pleased anyone or not. While the cask keeper approached, Han prepared the loan slip and asked the quiet driver to bring the two empty vessels where their issue marks could be read.

desert_p11_056.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_056.text: She had kept their lids attached with the original ties. The keeper approved that before looking at the linings. Too many useful loans returned as almost the same object, he said, with lids missing and owners expected to supply gratitude instead of parts. Han laughed and admitted he had made that complaint at his own yard. Yue watched an ordinary inspection give both men more pleasure than the provisional survey argument had managed all afternoon. The cask keeper arrived during the discussion. Han stopped talking long enough to return the two service casks in person.

desert_p11_057.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_057.text: Their issue marks matched his loan slip. Bao described their raw-water use and field rinse; the keeper inspected the linings and set them aside for full cleaning before another drinking transfer. He accepted the return, marked it complete, and handed Han the cancelled loan record. Yue watched the empty casks disappear into the store. The water they helped move remained with the caravan, while the borrowed capacity returned to the person who had provided it. One account had reached its actual end. The cancelled receipt carried a date and the keeper's clear initials.

desert_p11_058.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_058.text: Han showed it to the driver before filing it. The casks were now somebody else's next task, with their recent raw-water use recorded. The driver asked whether the next commission would buy dedicated containers. Gao said that was in the equipment proposal, subject to funding and actual load planning. The answer disappointed her slightly; she had enjoyed knowing exactly which casks would fit. The keeper said he would advise them on size without promising these particular vessels again. A successful loan could end without becoming a permanent invisible possession.

desert_p11_059.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_059.text: Before departure the clerk asked where to send the manager's fuller response. Han gave the Bitter Wells receiving house and the grass collective's messenger address, both already used in the current accounts. Gao wanted the diversion inspection order included if one was issued. Du wanted the older drainage sheet's source reference copied exactly. The clerk wrote each request on the cover page. Their different interests now pointed toward the same next document. Yue hoped it would arrive with more than a polite answer about correct forms.

desert_p11_060.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_060.text: Auntie Reed's cracked bowl had already performed enough public service for that kind of letter. Bao asked for news of the patient wagon. The clerk had received a message from its clinician at the southern halt: both guides remained stable, the injured leg supported, and the wagon would reach Bitter Wells after another gentle travel stretch. The note did not promise recovery or complete the clinic examination. Bao looked relieved by its particular facts. She copied the message destination so she could check in after the caravan returned. Tuo asked whether the mother had received the first notice.

desert_p11_061.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_061.text: The receiving house had acknowledged it. That answer let the guide sit back without inventing a reunion she had not seen. The cook purchased a little fresh onion from the quarry kitchen and paid from his recorded food allowance. He wanted the return supper to taste different from the outward one without making the new report finance a feast. Another kitchen worker asked whether they really found water at the old inn. He corrected the two sites more carefully than Han expected, using the names from Gao's figure. The rumour had already reached the stove.

desert_p11_062.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_062.text: Du wrote the correction on a small duplicate sheet for the kitchen wall, because hungry workers often read that wall more readily than the dispatch notice outside. Han declined the clerk's offer to store their original field case until the manager returned. They could provide copies while retaining the working originals for the cooperative and collective. The refusal was practical, not an accusation that the clerk intended theft. Several people needed the same evidence; one office should not become its only home merely because it had a dry cupboard. Gao prepared the copy package.

desert_p11_063.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_063.text: The clerk made a receipt listing exactly what he received. Yue saw how a public report could begin becoming public through several ordinary acts, each less dramatic than announcing that everyone deserved the truth. They rested long enough for the mules to drink and the injured ankle to settle after the ride. The caravan did not buy more water; the keeper's available clean stock was committed to the workers until the next scheduled delivery. Their measured return margin remained sufficient on the present route. Han asked him to warn other carriers that no casual resupply could be promised.

desert_p11_064.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_064.text: The keeper agreed. An eighty-litre surplus purchase several days earlier did not make the shed a well. Yue watched the six animals finish their troughs, then helped hang the emptied vessels where tomorrow's grit would not collect inside them. By the time they left the quarry yard, the afternoon had cooled enough for another ordinary stretch. Tuo gave the drivers the public ridge route toward the broken shelter, still riding. The clerk sent the manager's inspection request with a worker bound for the northern cut. Gao retained the dispatch-order copy and foreman's statement.

desert_p11_065.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_065.text: Du looked back at the kitchen's new two-site sheet, visible beside the onion price. The information had begun travelling through places people actually visited. Han counted all three carts as they cleared the gate and allowed himself a small satisfied breath. At the return camp beside the broken quarry shelter, the day's actual withdrawals closed at one hundred and seventy-eight litres. Eight hundred and eighty-three remained: three hundred and sixty in the first tank, two hundred and ninety in the second, and two hundred and thirty-three in the equipment cart's tank. The first tank still included its protected two hundred.

desert_p11_066.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_066.text: Han checked the figures against the drivers' depth readings, then shut the book for supper. The distribution would matter on the rougher return road. For the moment it meant nobody had to turn a cup into a debate. At camp Long Legs asked the cook whether roasted reed pith could join tomorrow's meal. The cook said he had learned the method, not purchased the whole northern crop. They had onions and their existing stores. He would use those before inventing a menu from an afternoon's pleasant sample. The driver looked disappointed, then asked whether onion skin was edible.

desert_p11_067.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_067.text: The cook told him to wait for the broth. Yue smiled at the boundary between learning and immediately converting knowledge into supply. Even a recipe had to meet what actually sat in the sacks. Bao cleaned Tuo's foot wrap and examined the skin where the support had pressed during riding. The ankle still required rest, but the cart had not worsened it noticeably. She altered one folded pad and asked the guide to report any numbness without waiting for a convenient halt. Tuo agreed, tired enough that the usual objection never arrived.

desert_p11_068.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_068.text: Du carried her cup over and placed it where the staff could not knock it down. She thanked him with no joke. The quiet exchange seemed more intimate than their long discussion of grief, because neither had prepared a sentence large enough to conceal it. Gao compared the caretaker receipts, dispatch order, and copied station column before packing the dry case. The papers covered different times and activities. A current maintenance visit did not reopen a loading hall; an old restriction did not automatically govern a repaired modern ridge; a new diversion did not prove its entire downstream course.

desert_p11_069.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_069.text: She arranged them by source and date, then asked Yue whether the sequence could be followed. The girl found one loose caption between two sheets. They tied it to the drawing it explained. The subscriber's earlier mistake had made that small connection worth unusual care. Han wrote a meeting request for the grass collective to hear the report as promised. It named the causeway, northern diversion, old store, and possible inspection funding, without asking the village to endorse an unseen carrier scheme. He would leave it when the return passed their yard.

desert_p11_070.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_070.text: Auntie Reed's nephew could bring the collective's own questions to Bitter Wells afterwards. Tuo approved the route and suggested the day their market wagon usually travelled. The arrangement used ordinary transport already available to the village. Nobody had to make a heroic journey merely to attend a conversation about their own ground. The farrier checked the six mules after feed. The brown pair's new lead loop had held through the day; he still kept the scuffed old piece separate for repair in town. Plum had worked without favouring a hoof.

desert_p11_071.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_071.text: The quiet driver brushed the sisters while the man with the wooden bird cleaned dust from his toy's reed opening. Yue helped shake grit from the empty flag case pockets. Camp chores felt easier when the day's main argument no longer stood in every doorway. The broken shelter's old ventilation duct began its thin note, a familiar sound without a new message. Du listened to the duct and said his revised essay should include Auntie Reed's maintenance crew. Gao agreed, provided he asked them how they wished the account told.

desert_p11_072.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_072.text: He said he had learned that lesson several times and found it distressingly capable of being learned again. Tuo offered him a bowl to hold while he suffered. He accepted it and asked whether her village would tolerate a map man at the tile table. She said they welcomed anyone who could lose with interest. He promised only interest. The return meeting had acquired one purpose that did not need an official agenda. Yue placed the reed ring on her knee and tried to copy its weave into the private notebook.

desert_p11_073.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_073.text: The loop looked simple until she followed the returning strip and lost which side passed under. She used the boy's actual object instead of drawing the knot she expected. The second attempt was better. A little gift could teach the same patience as a large station without becoming a symbol of the entire journey. She wrote the shelter location beside it so she might remember where to bring thanks if work carried her back. The note promised nothing beyond remembering. As the lamps went down, Han asked Gao whether the report had grown too complicated for the cooperative.

desert_p11_074.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_074.text: She said it could have a clear first page: use the ridge, keep loaded carts off the buried apron, inspect the new diversion downstream, and plan any reopening with the collective. The supporting pages would show why. He looked relieved. Complexity needed structure, not concealment. Yue heard the plain instructions and felt the day's scattered people gather into a route someone could follow. Beyond camp, the old shelter's note ended when the wind changed. The morning would still require ordinary eyes.

desert_p11_075.speaker: narrator
desert_p11_075.text: The cook's onion softened in the pot, giving the meal a smell Yue associated with rooms rather than open gravel. Tuo settled into her chair with the foot raised. Du placed the new source accounts beside the older tracings, a growing bundle that would take more than one comfortable sentence to explain in town. Gao watched the north sky, where cloud still held beyond the ridge without rain over camp. Yue put the reed ring beside the fish stone. Two people outside the dispatch ledger had changed the map more than another hour at the glass case would have done.
